blocks.content: Every load balancer needs to answer one question for each incoming request, which server gets this. The algorithm is the answer, and different algorithms make genuinely different trade-offs.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024006-236693344.png
blocks.alt: One question, answered differently by every algorithm covered in this topic

blocks.content: No single algorithm is best for every situation. The right choice depends on whether your servers are equal, how long requests actually take, whether session state matters, and how much overhead you can tolerate.

This topic builds directly on the earlier What are Load Balancers topic, which introduced these algorithms only briefly, here each one gets a genuine, worked-through explanation, including exactly when it is the right choice and when it quietly becomes the wrong one.
1. Round Robin
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396866291-398350474.png
blocks.alt: Requests distributed to servers in a fixed circular order, needing no memory beyond a simple pointer

blocks.content: The simplest algorithm. Requests are distributed to servers in a fixed circular order, server A, then B, then C, then back to A, needing no state beyond a pointer to the last server used. Each server gets an equal share of total requests.
Implementing it is genuinely as simple as it sounds, advancing an index by one and wrapping around with a modulo operation once it reaches the end of the server list.

Problem: server A is handling a ten second video transcode. Server B just finished in five milliseconds. Round robin still sends the next request to server A anyway, entirely blind to the fact that it is currently buried.
Best when all servers have equal specs and requests are roughly uniform in duration, the default, sensible choice for most simple, stateless HTTP reads.

Its simplicity is also exactly its limitation, round robin has no way of knowing that server A happens to be in the middle of an unusually slow request right now, it simply continues the fixed rotation regardless.
2. Weighted Round Robin
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274211203-824858663.png
blocks.alt: Traffic is split proportionally to each server's own configured capacity, not split evenly

blocks.content: Round robin, but each server carries a weight proportional to its own capacity. A server with weight 5 handles roughly five times more requests than one with weight 1, weights set manually based on the servers' actual hardware. Nginx implements this directly, its own weight setting controls how much traffic a given server receives proportionally.
Best when servers genuinely have different hardware specs, a newer, faster server added to an older pool, common during a phased hardware upgrade where old and new machines coexist temporarily.

Weights are typically set once, based on a known, measured difference in capacity, and rarely need to change unless the underlying hardware pool itself changes, unlike least connections, which naturally adapts as live traffic patterns shift.
3. Least Connections
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019242-549614152.png
blocks.alt: Rather than counting past requests, this algorithm looks at how many connections are genuinely active right now

blocks.content: Instead of counting total requests handled, this tracks active connections happening right now. Each new request goes to whichever server currently has the fewest open connections, adapting live to actual current load rather than a fixed rotation. Nginx's least_conn directive implements exactly this.
Best when request duration varies wildly, file uploads, video processing, complex database queries, any workload where some requests genuinely take ten times longer than others.

The trade-off is a small amount of extra bookkeeping, the load balancer has to track a live connection count per server and update it on every single request start and finish, a cost round robin never has to pay at all.
4. Weighted Least Connections
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024007-904106373.png
blocks.alt: Combining capacity and current load into one score picks the server that is both powerful and currently under-loaded

blocks.content: Combines weighted round robin with least connections. Rather than picking the server with the fewest raw connections, it picks the one with the best connections-to-weight ratio, dividing each server's current connection count by its own configured weight and choosing the smallest result. This balances current load and raw capacity together, HAProxy uses this as one of its core algorithms.
Best when servers have different capacities and requests have variable duration at the same time, the most capable, least busy server wins overall.

A tie in this ratio, two servers scoring equally well, is resolved by whichever tie-breaking rule the implementation chooses, commonly the first matching server found, exactly the same convention used throughout the examples in this topic.

This algorithm genuinely represents the more sophisticated end of the simple, connection-count-based family, correctly accounting for the two most common reasons a naive round robin fails: unequal hardware and unequal request duration, at the same time.
5. IP Hash
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274216319-827822174.png
blocks.alt: The exact same client IP always maps to the exact same server, with no session storage needed anywhere

blocks.content: The client's IP address is hashed and reduced to a server index, deterministically. The same IP always maps to the same server, guaranteed, without any session cookie or sticky session configuration at all, useful specifically when server-side session state genuinely needs stickiness without moving sessions to a shared store.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274217919-3772884.png
blocks.alt: Adding or removing even one server reshuffles nearly every client's assignment at once, a genuinely disruptive side effect

blocks.content: If a server goes down, every user hashed to it gets errors, and the overall distribution shifts unevenly. Adding or removing a server rehashes essentially everything, users bounce to entirely new servers all at once, exactly the problem consistent hashing exists to solve.

Best when server-side sessions genuinely exist and stickiness is needed without Redis, though the better long-term fix, covered in the previous topic, is usually moving sessions to a shared store and using least connections instead.

IP hash also has a subtler downside worth knowing, many users behind the same corporate network address translation, covered in the NAT and Firewalls topic, all share one public IP, and IP hash sends every one of them to the exact same server, potentially overloading it while others sit comparatively idle.
6. Consistent Hashing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274219600-160738704.png
blocks.alt: Both servers and requests are placed on the same conceptual ring, with each request served by the first server found going clockwise

blocks.content: The smarter version of IP hash. Servers and requests are both placed on a virtual ring, and each request goes to the first server found clockwise from its own position on that ring.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024005-221550561.png
blocks.alt: Adding a new server moves only the small slice of requests that now fall closer to it, everything else stays exactly where it already was

blocks.content: With plain hashing, adding or removing one server out of three reassigns essentially all requests. With consistent hashing, roughly only one over N of them move, the rest stay on their original server completely undisturbed. This matters enormously for cache-based systems specifically, since every request that stays put is one less cache miss during a scaling event.

Best when distributing across cache servers like Memcached or a Redis cluster, or any distributed database, where minimizing cache invalidation during node additions or removals is genuinely critical.

Real implementations rarely place just one point per server on the ring, they place many virtual points per server instead, spreading each server's own share of the ring more evenly and avoiding one unlucky server ending up responsible for a disproportionately large arc purely by chance.

This same underlying ring concept reappears throughout distributed systems well beyond load balancing itself, distributed caches and distributed databases alike lean on it specifically because minimizing disruption during scaling matters just as much for them as it does here.
7. Least Response Time
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274223348-613555779.png
blocks.alt: Combining current load with actual measured speed picks the server that is genuinely fastest right now, not just least busy

blocks.content: Combines active connection count with a server's own average response time. The server with the lowest product of response time multiplied by active connections wins, genuinely the fastest, least loaded option, not just the one with fewer open connections.

This distinction matters concretely, a server with very few connections but a genuinely slow average response time, perhaps struggling with a resource issue of its own, is correctly avoided here, exactly the case plain least connections alone would miss entirely.

Best when latency is a hard requirement, financial trading systems, real-time bidding, live gaming, HAProxy calls this leastconn with latency tracking, and it is generally the most sophisticated of the algorithms covered here.

Tracking a live, continuously updated average response time per server adds real bookkeeping overhead, worth paying specifically when the cost of a slow response genuinely outweighs the cost of the extra tracking itself, not for every ordinary workload by default.
8. Power of Two Choices
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274225050-277770224.png
blocks.alt: Comparing just two randomly picked servers, rather than every server or none at all, gives nearly optimal balancing for almost no cost

blocks.content: A genuinely clever insight from distributed systems research. Rather than checking every single server, expensive at scale, or picking one purely at random, dumb, this randomly picks exactly two servers and sends the request to whichever of those two currently has fewer connections.

This algorithm is a genuine highlight of the whole field precisely because it trades almost nothing, two quick comparisons instead of one, for an enormous, mathematically provable improvement in worst-case balance across the entire pool.

Pure random choice can leave load meaningfully uneven, with maximum load growing roughly as log n over log log n. Comparing just two random choices dramatically improves this, to roughly log log n, near-optimal balancing for the cost of comparing only two servers instead of scanning the entire pool.

Used by Nginx's least_conn on large pools, Envoy's own default, and AWS load balancers, all rely on variants of this exact idea, valuable specifically once a pool grows into the hundreds of servers, where scanning every one for the true minimum becomes genuinely expensive.

The elegance here is genuinely surprising, doubling the number of random candidates checked, from one to two, produces a dramatically better mathematical guarantee, while checking three, four, or more candidates keeps improving the guarantee only marginally from that point on, which is exactly why two, not three or five, became the standard choice in real, production implementations.

The example below implements exactly the consistent hashing concept described earlier: placing servers on a ring, assigning a set of keys to whichever server sits next clockwise, then adding a new server and confirming only a small fraction of keys actually move, contrasted directly against plain modulo hashing, where changing the server count reshuffles nearly everything.

codes.python:
MOD = 1_000_000_007
import bisect


def djb2_hash(s):
    hash_value = 5381
    for ch in s:
        hash_value = ((hash_value * 33) + ord(ch)) % MOD
    # Plain djb2 barely spreads strings that share a prefix and differ only in
    # a trailing digit, like key1, key2, key3, so a finishing mix step (the
    # same style murmur3 uses) is needed before the hash is fit onto the ring.
    hash_value ^= (hash_value >> 15)
    hash_value = (hash_value * 2246822519) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    hash_value ^= (hash_value >> 13)
    hash_value = (hash_value * 3266489917) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    hash_value ^= (hash_value >> 16)
    return hash_value


class ConsistentHashRing:
    # A simplified consistent hashing ring: servers and keys share the same hash
    # space, and each key is served by the first server found clockwise from it.
    def __init__(self):
        self.positions = []
        self.ring = {}

    def add_server(self, name):
        position = djb2_hash(name) % 3600
        self.ring[position] = name
        self.positions = sorted(self.ring.keys())

    def get_server(self, key):
        position = djb2_hash(key) % 3600
        idx = bisect.bisect_left(self.positions, position)
        if idx == len(self.positions):
            idx = 0
        return self.ring[self.positions[idx]]


def main():
    keys = [f"key{i}" for i in range(1, 31)]

    ring = ConsistentHashRing()
    ring.add_server("A")
    ring.add_server("B")
    ring.add_server("C")

    before = {key: ring.get_server(key) for key in keys}

    ring.add_server("D")

    moved = sum(1 for key in keys if ring.get_server(key) != before[key])
    print(f"Consistent hashing: after adding server D, {moved} out of {len(keys)} keys moved")

    plain_moved = 0
    for key in keys:
        h = djb2_hash(key)
        old_index = h % 3
        new_index = h % 4
        if old_index != new_index:
            plain_moved += 1
    print(f"Plain modulo hashing: going from 3 to 4 servers, {plain_moved} out of {len(keys)} keys moved")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

10. A Decision Framework
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019240-263874067.png
blocks.alt: Two honest questions about your own servers and requests narrow the choice down considerably before anything else needs to be considered

blocks.content: Two questions cut through most of the decision immediately: do your servers actually have different capacities, and does request duration genuinely vary. If both are true, weighted least connections. If only capacity differs, weighted round robin. If only duration varies, least connections. If neither is true, plain round robin is entirely sufficient, and reaching for anything more sophisticated adds complexity without adding real benefit.

IP hash, consistent hashing, least response time, and power of two choices sit outside this basic framework entirely, each answering a more specific need, session stickiness, cache-cluster stability, hard latency requirements, or very large pools, layered on top of whichever base algorithm the two questions above already pointed toward.
11. A Common Mistake: Round Robin With Variable Request Duration
blocks.text: 11. A Common Mistake: Round Robin With Variable Request Duration

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274228148-377823391.png
blocks.alt: Round robin has no awareness at all of how busy a server currently is, only whose turn it is next

blocks.content: A frequent mistake is defaulting to round robin for a workload where request duration genuinely varies a lot, some quick reads, some heavy report generation. Round robin has no concept of how busy a server actually is right now, it simply continues its fixed rotation, cheerfully sending the next request to a server already buried in a slow task while a genuinely free server sits idle.

The fix here costs almost nothing, switching to least connections requires no new infrastructure, just a different, already-available algorithm setting, making this one of the cheapest, highest-leverage changes a struggling system can make.
12. A Common Mistake: Plain IP Hash for a Cache Cluster
blocks.text: 12. A Common Mistake: Plain IP Hash for a Cache Cluster

blocks.content: Using plain IP hash, or an equivalent simple modulo scheme, to distribute keys across a cache cluster is a common but costly mistake. Every time the cluster scales up or down, nearly every key's assignment changes at once, causing a massive, avoidable wave of cache misses right when the system is already under the pressure of a scaling event. Consistent hashing exists specifically to prevent this.

This mistake is especially easy to make precisely because plain modulo hashing works perfectly well right up until the very first scaling event, giving no warning signal at all that a much more disruptive failure mode is waiting for the first time the cluster actually needs to grow or shrink.
Worked Example

A team runs a Redis cache cluster behind a load balancer using plain modulo hashing across three nodes. Adding a fourth node during a traffic spike accidentally causes a massive wave of cache misses, since nearly every key's node assignment just changed, hitting the origin database hard at the exact moment it could least afford it.

The same team, separately, runs a fleet of API servers with genuinely identical hardware and roughly uniform request duration, and deliberately keeps plain round robin there, resisting the temptation to add unnecessary sophistication where the two decision questions from earlier both clearly point toward the simplest option.

Switching to consistent hashing fixes this permanently, the next time a node is added, only the small slice of keys genuinely closest to that new node on the ring actually move, every other key continues being served from cache exactly as before, with no disruptive wave of misses at all.

This exact scenario, and its fix, is precisely what the code demonstration earlier in this topic verified concretely: a genuinely small number of keys moving under consistent hashing, contrasted directly against nearly all of them moving under plain modulo hashing given the exact same change in server count.
Common Mistakes

["Defaulting to round robin for a workload where request duration genuinely varies a great deal, rather than reaching for least connections","Using plain IP hash or simple modulo hashing across a cache cluster, causing a massive rebalancing wave every time the cluster scales","Assuming weighted algorithms are only useful during a temporary hardware migration, when they remain the right permanent choice for any pool with genuinely mixed server capacities","Reaching for the most sophisticated algorithm, like least response time, everywhere by default, when a much simpler algorithm would have been entirely sufficient and easier to reason about","Placing only a single point per server on a consistent hashing ring, letting one unlucky server end up responsible for a disproportionately large, unbalanced share of the ring purely by chance"]

Using plain IP hash or simple modulo hashing across a cache cluster, causing a massive rebalancing wave every time the cluster scales
Assuming weighted algorithms are only useful during a temporary hardware migration, when they remain the right permanent choice for any pool with genuinely mixed server capacities

blocks.content: Practice

For each of the following, choose the single best fitting algorithm and justify it in one sentence: a stateless API where every request takes roughly the same time, a video transcoding service where jobs vary from seconds to minutes, a Redis cluster expected to scale up and down regularly, and a real-time bidding system where every millisecond of latency matters.
Then trace through a small consistent hashing ring with four servers and eight keys by hand, add a fifth server, and count exactly how many keys actually moved.

Finally, work through the decision framework from earlier in this topic on your own current system, or a hypothetical one, and check whether the algorithm it actually uses today matches what those two questions would have recommended.
Key Takeaway

Every load balancing algorithm answers the same question, which server gets this request, but each one optimizes for something different. Round robin and weighted round robin are simple and fast but blind to real-time load. Least connections and weighted least connections adapt to genuinely variable request duration. IP hash gives cheap stickiness but rebalances badly, exactly the problem consistent hashing solves for cache and database clusters. Least response time and power of two choices are the most sophisticated options, worth their added complexity specifically when latency is critical or the server pool is genuinely large. Choosing correctly starts with being honest about whether your servers are equal, whether requests take similar time, and whether minimizing rebalancing disruption actually matters for your workload.

None of these algorithms is a permanent, unchangeable choice either, as a system's own traffic patterns and server pool genuinely evolve, revisiting this same decision framework periodically is worth doing, rather than assuming whatever was chosen at launch remains the right choice forever.
